title: Supervised Fine-Tuning
summary: SFT teaches a pretrained model to produce desired responses under a clearly defined conditioning format.

sections.title: From text prediction to task behavior
paragraphs: Pretraining learns patterns across broad text distributions. Supervised fine-tuning continues likelihood training on examples organized around desired tasks, instructions, or conversations. The underlying next-token objective need not change, but the data distribution and loss mask usually do. An instruction dataset tells the model which response patterns should follow particular prompts. It does not automatically provide feedback about alternative responses that were never included.

sections.title: Define exactly which tokens are targets
paragraphs: For a prompt \(x\) and response \(y\), the usual response objective is \(-\sum_t\log p_\theta(y_t\mid x,y_{<t})\). Prompt tokens supply context; assistant-response tokens receive loss. In multi-turn data, the chosen chat template and mask determine which turns are supervised. Padding must be excluded, and truncation must not silently remove most answers. If examples have different lengths, token-weighted and example-weighted averages optimize different objectives, so document the reduction used.

sections.title: Build a small trustworthy pipeline
paragraphs: Inspect decoded input sequences and highlighted target positions before launching a large run. A misplaced delimiter can teach the model to emit role markers or train on user text unintentionally. Compare held-out instruction behavior, not only training loss, and check for overlap between source conversations and evaluation prompts. Preserve useful pretrained behavior by monitoring broader tasks. Better formatting compliance can coexist with weaker factual performance, so avoid treating one benchmark improvement as evidence that every capability improved.

sections.title: Reading the paper: identify the supervised target
paragraphs: In Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback, distinguish supervised demonstrations from preference comparisons and policy-generated rollouts. They support different objectives. The supervised stage learns token probabilities for demonstrated responses conditioned on prompts, not a scalar judgment of every possible answer.

Imagine two training answers with ten and one hundred target tokens. A token-mean objective gives the longer answer more aggregate influence than an equal-per-sequence mean. Neither reduction is inherently universal, but switching between them changes which examples drive learning. Prompt and padding masks further determine the effective supervision.

Inspect a decoded training example alongside its label mask and shifted targets. Verify that the model predicts each response token from the intended preceding context, including any end-of-response marker. Then compare held-out loss with generated-answer behavior: fitting demonstrations establishes conditional imitation, while helpfulness and factual reliability still require appropriate evaluations.

exercise.prompt: A training sample contains 100 prompt tokens and 20 assistant tokens. Which positions usually contribute to response-only SFT loss?
exercise.answer: The 20 assistant target positions contribute, including any intended end-of-response target according to the template. Prompt tokens remain visible as context but are masked from this response-only loss; padding is also masked.

takeaways: SFT behavior depends strongly on data and formatting.
Inspect token masks and loss reductions explicitly.

references.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback
references.note: Separate demonstration learning, preference modeling, and policy optimization.

title: Teacher Forcing and Exposure Bias
summary: Training on reference prefixes and generating from model prefixes create different conditioning distributions.

sections.title: The prefix changes the problem
paragraphs: With teacher forcing, a model predicts the next reference token given earlier reference tokens. During generation, earlier tokens come from the model itself. A small mistake can create a prefix that was rare in the training set, and later predictions must cope with that unfamiliar context. This difference is often called exposure bias. It is a distribution mismatch, not proof that maximum-likelihood training is inherently useless or mathematically invalid.

sections.title: Follow a branching sequence
paragraphs: Suppose the reference begins 'The answer is five.' Training the token after 'answer' conditions on that correct prefix. At inference the model may instead produce 'The estimate seems', after which the appropriate continuation changes. Per-token accuracy measured only under reference prefixes does not fully capture recovery from this branch. Teacher forcing remains computationally convenient: a causal mask allows many reference-conditioned token predictions to be evaluated in parallel while preventing access to future targets.

sections.title: Evaluate the behavior you need
paragraphs: Measure free-running generations as well as teacher-forced validation loss. Include tasks where an early error changes later constraints, and inspect whether the model can recover. Training on generated prefixes or collecting corrective feedback can address parts of the mismatch, but each method introduces its own objective and data-collection assumptions. Simply replacing reference tokens with arbitrary samples can make targets inconsistent. Keep teacher forcing distinct from knowledge distillation: the former describes conditioning during sequence training, while the latter describes transferring a teacher's information.

sections.title: Reading the paper: who supplies the prefix?
paragraphs: In On-Policy Distillation of Language Models, focus on the prefixes at which the teacher supervises the student. Teacher forcing on reference sequences and supervision on student-generated sequences expose different contexts, even if both use a token-level distribution-matching loss.

Suppose a reference answer begins with the correct city, but the student often generates a different city first. Training only on the reference continuation never directly teaches recovery from that common student prefix. Querying the teacher there changes the state distribution of training, not merely the final answer label.

Design a diagnostic that records the first divergence and evaluates subsequent continuations from both reference and sampled prefixes. Some generated prefixes may already make the original task impossible to recover cleanly, so teacher quality on those contexts also matters. On-policy supervision addresses a distribution mismatch; it does not guarantee that every self-generated mistake becomes a useful lesson.

exercise.prompt: Can excellent teacher-forced next-token accuracy guarantee that a long generated sequence is correct?
exercise.answer: No. Generation may enter prefixes absent from the validation conditioning distribution, and even small local error probabilities can accumulate across many decisions. Evaluate complete outputs and recovery behavior rather than relying on a local metric alone.

takeaways: Reference prefixes and generated prefixes are different data.
Check complete trajectories in addition to local predictions.

references.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes
references.note: Compare student-generated contexts with fixed teacher demonstrations.

title: The Teacher and Student in Distillation
summary: Distillation transfers selected behavior while the student's architecture and training distribution determine what can be retained.

sections.title: Specify the transfer contract
paragraphs: A teacher is a source of supervision, not necessarily a single larger network. It can be an ensemble, a specialized model, or a system with additional computation. A student learns a cheaper or differently structured approximation. The contract must identify inputs, available teacher signals, and target deployment conditions. Without that contract, statements such as 'the student learned the teacher' hide which behaviors were actually measured.

sections.title: Match on an explicit distribution
paragraphs: For inputs \(x\) sampled from a chosen distribution \(D\), a logit objective may minimize \(\mathbb{E}_{x\sim D}\!\left[\operatorname{KL}\!\left(p_T(\cdot\mid x)\|p_S(\cdot\mid x)\right)\right]\). The input distribution matters as much as the divergence: a student trained only on short arithmetic prompts has little direct supervision for long documents. Sequence-response distillation instead trains on teacher-produced outputs, often losing access to uncertainty over other answers. A smaller student can approximate easy regions well while lacking capacity to reproduce every teacher distinction.

sections.title: Audit teacher errors and student gains
paragraphs: Hold out evaluation examples before collecting teacher labels. Record teacher settings, sampling choices, filtering rules, and the cost of producing the dataset. Compare the distilled student with an equally sized student trained on ordinary labels using a comparable budget. A student can outperform a teacher on a narrow metric through regularization or data selection, but this is an empirical outcome rather than a general guarantee. Inspect inherited mistakes and unsupported confidence instead of assuming teacher-generated text is ground truth.

sections.title: Reading the paper: teacher information is a resource
paragraphs: In Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network, compare the teacher's soft distribution with its winning label. The extra supervision lies in relative alternatives. Whether a student benefits depends on the relevance of those alternatives and the capacity available to represent them.

Suppose a teacher distributes probability among several semantically similar classes, while the dataset supplies only one label. Matching that distribution can teach relationships absent from the label. If the teacher's alternatives reflect a spurious background correlation, however, matching them can transfer the same weakness.

Evaluate the teacher on the student's intended inputs, including rare groups and shifted domains, before interpreting imitation as improvement. Record which teacher signals are available and how expensive they are to obtain. A stronger teacher benchmark score alone does not establish that its distribution is the best target for a smaller model under a different deployment budget.

exercise.prompt: Two students use the same teacher and loss, but one sees only easy prompts. Are their distillation problems equivalent?
exercise.answer: No. Their training input distributions differ, so the expected objectives emphasize different regions. The easy-prompt student may match the teacher there while remaining unconstrained on harder or longer inputs.

takeaways: Define the teacher signal and input distribution.
Compare against a budget-matched student baseline.

references.title: Distilling the Knowledge in a Neural Network
references.note: Read the soft-target objective and temperature discussion.

title: Offline and On-Policy Distillation
summary: The source of prefixes determines whether a student learns on fixed demonstrations or on states its own policy visits.

sections.title: Ask who generated the context
paragraphs: Offline distillation uses a fixed collection of teacher outputs or other prepared examples. On-policy distillation obtains contexts or trajectories from the current student and asks the teacher to supervise those visited states. The latter can expose the teacher to the student's own mistakes and unusual prefixes. This distinction concerns data collection. It does not, by itself, determine whether the matching loss is forward KL, reverse KL, or token likelihood.

sections.title: Trace one training iteration
paragraphs: An offline loop samples a stored prompt-response pair and updates the student. An on-policy loop samples a prompt, lets the student generate a continuation, obtains teacher information at selected student prefixes, and updates using that feedback. The teacher might provide a distribution over next tokens or a corrected continuation. If a prefix is already inconsistent, a teacher completion should be interpreted as a response to that actual prefix, not as a label for an unrelated reference context.

sections.title: Account for freshness and cost
paragraphs: After enough student updates, previously collected trajectories are no longer sampled from the current policy. Reusing them creates off-policy or stale-data considerations, even if they originally came from the student. Record rollout-policy versions, sampling settings, teacher-query cost, and the ratio of collected to reused data. Compare methods at matched total budgets, since on-policy collection can consume significant generation compute. Evaluate both ordinary task performance and behavior after plausible mistakes; a lower teacher-matching loss alone does not show better free-running behavior.

sections.title: Reading the paper: separate rollout policy from matching loss
paragraphs: In On-Policy Distillation of Language Models, identify the student-generated contexts and the teacher distribution evaluated at those contexts. Then inspect the divergence used to train the student. Changing the context distribution and changing the divergence are separate experimental choices.

Imagine collecting student rollouts once and training on them for many epochs. The first update uses contexts generated by the current student; later updates increasingly use contexts from an older version. Calling the entire run on-policy without specifying refresh frequency obscures that growing mismatch.

Compare fixed teacher-generated data, periodically refreshed student data, and a mixture under a matched teacher-query budget. Track whether the teacher remains reliable on unusual student prefixes. The supervised token loss can backpropagate through student probabilities while treating sampled tokens as fixed data; this should not be confused with automatically differentiating the discrete rollout or adding a REINFORCE estimator.

exercise.prompt: A student generates a dataset once, then trains on it for many changing policy versions. Is every later update strictly on-policy?
exercise.answer: No. The dataset reflects the policy that collected it. Later policies induce different trajectory distributions, so the fixed collection becomes stale relative to them unless the method explicitly accounts for that mismatch.

takeaways: Data collection and divergence direction are separate choices.
Track the policy version behind each rollout.

references.title: On-Policy Distillation of Language Models: Learning from Self-Generated Mistakes

title: Forward KL and Reverse KL
summary: The order of the distributions changes which mismatches receive strong penalties.

sections.title: Name both distributions first
paragraphs: Let \(p\) be a teacher or target distribution and \(q\) the student approximation. Forward KL commonly means \(\operatorname{KL}(p\|q)\), while reverse KL means \(\operatorname{KL}(q\|p)\); always declare this convention. The terms are not symmetric distances. Forward KL averages \(\log\frac{p}{q}\) under \(p\), so it strongly penalizes assigning tiny \(q\) probability where \(p\) has mass. Reverse KL averages \(\log\frac{q}{p}\) under \(q\), emphasizing locations the student itself chooses to occupy.

sections.title: Work through a two-outcome example
paragraphs: Take \(p=(0.5,0.5)\) and \(q=(0.9,0.1)\). Forward KL is \(0.5\log\frac{0.5}{0.9}+0.5\log\frac{0.5}{0.1}\), approximately 0.511 nats. Reverse KL is \(0.9\log\frac{0.9}{0.5}+0.1\log\frac{0.1}{0.5}\), approximately 0.368 nats. Both are zero only when the distributions agree. If \(q\) is exactly zero on positive \(p\) mass, forward KL is infinite; the analogous support issue reverses when \(p\) is zero on positive \(q\) mass.

sections.title: Use mode intuitions carefully
paragraphs: Forward KL is often called coverage-seeking and reverse KL mode-seeking when a restricted approximation cannot represent a multimodal target. These are useful tendencies, not unconditional laws about every neural model. If \(q\) can equal \(p\) and optimization succeeds, both objectives share that optimum. Sampling distributions also matter: an estimator for one expectation cannot be reused for the other without appropriate weighting or a different derivation. In language models, distinguish token-level conditional KL from KL over entire sequence distributions.

sections.title: Reading the sources: write the expectation's distribution
paragraphs: Read the KL definition in Deep Learning together with the divergence choices in On-Policy Distillation of Language Models. For every expression, label which distribution supplies the expectation and which receives the logarithmic penalty. Forward and reverse are incomplete names unless their arguments are explicit.

Suppose \(p\) assigns probability to two distant modes and \(q\) can represent only one narrow component. Penalizing missing \(p\) mass can encourage \(q\) to broaden, while penalizing \(q\) mass where \(p\) is tiny can encourage a focused solution. These are consequences of support and model constraints, not universal behaviors of every optimization landscape.

Compute both divergences on a small categorical example before applying the intuition to sequences. At the token level, also state which prefixes are sampled; reversing KL at fixed prefixes is different from changing the prefix distribution. Smoothing zeros makes some expressions finite, but it changes the objective and should be documented.

exercise.prompt: If \(p=(1,0)\) and \(q=(0.5,0.5)\), which KL is infinite?
exercise.answer: \(\operatorname{KL}(q\|p)\) is infinite because \(q\) assigns positive mass to an outcome where \(p\) is zero. \(\operatorname{KL}(p\|q)=\log 2\) is finite, using the convention that zero-weighted terms contribute zero.

takeaways: Write the ordered KL expression explicitly.
Mode-seeking language depends on approximation constraints.

title: Jensen–Shannon Divergence and Distribution Matching
summary: Jensen–Shannon divergence compares distributions symmetrically; exact evaluation and estimation from samples require different information and assumptions.

sections.title: Compare through a shared mixture
paragraphs: For distributions \(p\) and \(q\), define \(m=\frac{p+q}{2}\). Jensen–Shannon divergence is half \(\operatorname{KL}(p\|m)\) plus half \(\operatorname{KL}(q\|m)\). Each distribution is compared with a mixture that contains its own support, avoiding the infinite-support penalty possible in one-way KL. With natural logarithms, JS lies between zero and \(\log 2\). The square root of JS is a metric; JS itself should not casually be called a distance satisfying every metric property.

sections.title: Inspect an extreme example
paragraphs: If \(p\) puts all mass on one outcome and \(q\) puts all mass on another, their mixture assigns half to each. Both component KL values equal \(\log 2\), so JS reaches \(\log 2\). If \(p=q\), the mixture is identical and JS is zero. This symmetry can be useful when neither distribution is naturally privileged. However, a bounded divergence can have very different optimization behavior from a directional KL, particularly when parameterized distributions barely overlap.

sections.title: Connect the objective to accessible signals
paragraphs: Matching sampled outputs, matching token probabilities, and matching feature distributions are different operations. A finite batch of text samples does not reveal every sequence probability. Density-ratio estimation or other surrogate objectives may be needed when probabilities are unavailable, and those introduce assumptions. Choose a divergence based on what errors matter and what can be estimated reliably. Monitor task outcomes as well as the matching statistic; two systems can agree on common outputs while missing rare but important cases.

sections.title: Reading the papers: ideal distribution matching and a metric
paragraphs: In Generative Adversarial Networks, inspect the distribution comparison obtained after optimizing the discriminator. Then read Endres and Schindelin for the separate metric property of the square-root construction. These are different results; neither makes a finite discriminator's training loss an exact measured divergence.

Use three simple categorical distributions to distinguish symmetry from metric structure. Symmetry merely says exchanging \(p\) and \(q\) leaves the result unchanged. A metric also needs the triangle inequality, which cannot be established by checking that JS is bounded or by displaying a few symmetric examples.

For empirical distributions with large or continuous supports, decide whether you have normalized probabilities, samples, or an estimated density ratio. Each permits different calculations and introduces different errors. Report the estimator and held-out procedure alongside the number. A small matching statistic is informative only relative to the representation and distributions that were actually compared.

exercise.prompt: For \(p=(1,0)\) and \(q=(0,1)\), compute JS using base-2 logarithms.
exercise.answer: The mixture is \((0.5,0.5)\), each component KL is 1 bit, and JS is 1 bit. The numerical upper bound changes with logarithm base; the underlying comparison does not.

takeaways: JS compares both distributions with their mixture.
A computable surrogate is not automatically the exact divergence.

title: Reward Models and Preference Models
summary: A learned score summarizes observed comparisons and can fail outside the conditions that produced those comparisons.

sections.title: Learn from relative judgments
paragraphs: A preference dataset may contain a prompt and two candidate responses with a preferred choice. A reward model maps a prompt-response pair to a scalar used to predict such choices. Under a common Bradley–Terry formulation, \(P(y_A\text{ preferred to }y_B)=\sigma\!\left(r(x,y_A)-r(x,y_B)\right)\). The model learns score differences from comparison labels. Adding the same constant to both scores leaves that preference probability unchanged, so the absolute score has no intrinsic universal meaning.

sections.title: Trace a concrete pair
paragraphs: Suppose a model gives response A score 2 and response B score 0. Their predicted preference probability is \(\sigma(2)\), about 0.881. Training increases this probability when A is labeled preferred. Annotators may favor correctness, clarity, brevity, or style in different proportions, and disagreement can be genuine. Pair construction matters: comparing obviously bad answers teaches a different boundary from comparing two strong but subtly different answers.

sections.title: Evaluate beyond pair accuracy
paragraphs: Split data to avoid repeated prompts or near-duplicate responses crossing train and test boundaries. Inspect performance by task type, length, and annotator group when available. A policy optimized against the learned score can discover shortcuts such as verbosity or formatting that correlate with preferences in training but do not reflect actual usefulness. Maintain an independent evaluation process, document label instructions, and check whether score improvements correspond to human judgments on newly generated outputs. Reward-model confidence is not a certificate of factual truth.

sections.title: Reading the paper: reward differences are identifiable
paragraphs: In Training Language Models to Follow Instructions with Human Feedback, connect preference comparisons to the reward-model training objective. A pairwise model predicts which response is preferred from a difference of scores. Its outputs are not automatically probabilities of truth or universal quality units.

Add ten to every candidate's reward for one prompt. The pairwise probabilities remain unchanged because the offset cancels. Multiplying all scores by ten, however, sharpens those probabilities and changes calibration. This separates an unidentifiable location shift from a scale that matters to the preference likelihood and downstream optimization.

Inspect labeling criteria, disagreement, and prompt distribution before treating reward as an external ground truth. Test comparisons on responses produced by the policy being optimized, not only on the reward model's original dataset. A policy can find inputs where the learned ranking extrapolates poorly, making held-out preference accuracy an incomplete guarantee of safe optimization.

exercise.prompt: If every reward score increases by 100, do Bradley–Terry pair probabilities change?
exercise.answer: No. The difference \(r_A-r_B\) remains unchanged, so the sigmoid probability is identical. This illustrates why pairwise data identifies relative scores more directly than an absolute reward scale.

takeaways: Preference labels define a measurement process.
Validate rewards on fresh policy-generated responses.

title: States, Actions, Rewards, and Policies
summary: An RL problem specifies how decisions change future situations and which cumulative outcomes are valued.

sections.title: Describe the interaction
paragraphs: An agent receives information, chooses an action, and observes a transition and reward. The state is a representation sufficient for predicting relevant future dynamics under actions; the observation may reveal only part of that state. A policy maps available information to an action distribution or deterministic action. Reward is an immediate signal, while return combines rewards across time. Confusing reward with return hides the delayed consequences that make sequential decisions challenging.

sections.title: Build a tiny example
paragraphs: In a two-room task, the state includes room location and whether a key has been collected. Actions move, wait, or pick up the key. A reward of one occurs only after opening the locked exit. The discounted return is \(G_t=\sum_k\gamma^k r_{t+k}\), with \(\gamma\) between zero and one in the usual discounted setting. A policy that repeatedly takes an immediately convenient action may never reach the exit, even though a longer key-collecting sequence succeeds.

sections.title: Make the language-model analogy precise
paragraphs: For autoregressive text, the prefix can serve as the decision context and the next token as an action. A final answer score can be a terminal reward. The environment and termination rules must still be specified, especially when tools or external feedback are involved. A preference score is one possible reward source, not a required component of RL. Before choosing an algorithm, write down observations, actions, transition timing, reward rules, episode endings, and the actual evaluation metric.

sections.title: Reading the documentation: define the interaction boundary
paragraphs: In Spinning Up's Key Concepts in RL, follow the distinction among observations, states, actions, and returns. These definitions specify what information the policy receives and which consequences the objective values. The same physical problem can yield different learning tasks under different observation boundaries.

For a language model, a prompt and generated prefix can serve as an observation, a token as an action, and a completed response as the point where reward arrives. In a tool-using setting, external results also affect later observations. Token count alone does not describe the environmental interaction.

Construct a short trajectory and label reward timing explicitly before introducing discounting. A reward indexed after an action may appear with a different subscript in another source without changing the underlying convention. State whether the horizon terminates naturally or is truncated, because a cutoff and a terminal state can require different value-estimation treatment.

exercise.prompt: A trajectory receives rewards 0, 0, and 1 with \(\gamma=0.9\). What is the return from the first decision under the stated indexing?
exercise.answer: It is \(0+0.9\times0+0.9^2\times1=0.81\). Discounting reduces the contribution of delayed reward; using \(\gamma=1\) would make this return equal to 1.

takeaways: Specify the interaction before selecting an algorithm.
Immediate reward and cumulative return are different quantities.

references.title: Spinning Up: Key Concepts in RL
references.note: Review trajectories, policies, returns, and value functions.

title: Policy Gradients and REINFORCE
summary: The log-probability trick lets sampled rewards guide a stochastic policy without differentiating through the environment.

sections.title: Differentiate the sampling distribution
paragraphs: An action sample is discrete or produced through dynamics that may not be differentiable. REINFORCE instead differentiates the probability assigned to the sampled trajectory. For \(J(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{\tau\sim\pi_\theta}[R(\tau)]\), a basic estimator is \(R(\tau)\nabla_\theta\log p_\theta(\tau)\). When environment transitions do not depend on \(\theta\), the parameter-dependent terms are policy action probabilities. Successful sampled choices are made more likely, while below-baseline outcomes can push their probabilities down.

sections.title: Follow a Bernoulli bandit
paragraphs: Let a policy choose action 1 with probability \(p=\sigma(z)\). Suppose action 1 returns reward 1 and action 0 returns 0. The expected reward is \(p\), whose derivative with respect to \(z\) is \(p(1-p)\). A sampled score-function update uses \(R(a)(a-p)\). Its expectation matches the derivative, although individual samples vary. In a sequential task, replace the single log probability with a sum of action log probabilities and use appropriate returns or advantages.

sections.title: Implement the estimator faithfully
paragraphs: A common minimization loss is \(-\operatorname{stop\_gradient}(\text{return}-\text{baseline})\times\text{log\_probability}\). Do not backpropagate through a reward estimate accidentally unless the algorithm explicitly requires that pathway. Log probabilities must correspond to the distribution that sampled actions; changing temperature or truncating support can alter that distribution. REINFORCE can be unbiased under its assumptions while still having high variance and poor sample efficiency. Use repeated runs, reward diagnostics, and simple bandits to verify signs before applying it to long sequences.

sections.title: Reading the derivation: differentiate probability, not sampled text
paragraphs: In Spinning Up's policy-gradient derivation, expand the trajectory probability before applying the log-derivative identity. Shared environment factors do not contribute parameter derivatives when the environment is independent of policy parameters. The resulting estimator weights policy log-probability gradients by sampled returns.

For a binary action with probability \(p\), the logit derivative of its log probability is \(a-p\). With reward one for action one and zero otherwise, the expected weighted derivative is \(p(1-p)\). At \(p=0.5\), the two sampled contributions are 0.5 and zero, whose average under the policy is 0.25.

This example distinguishes a correct stochastic estimator from a deterministic gradient on each sample. Check the gradient-descent loss sign and detach sampled returns when implementing the basic estimator. Also confirm how data were collected; a mathematically correct log-probability expression evaluated on another behavior distribution need not estimate the desired on-policy gradient.

exercise.prompt: In the Bernoulli example, \(p=0.5\) and action 1 receives reward 1. What is the sampled gradient with respect to \(z\)?
exercise.answer: It is \(1\times(1-0.5)=0.5\) for gradient ascent. Increasing \(z\) raises the probability of action 1. The sampled value need not equal the expected gradient, which is 0.25 at \(p=0.5\).

takeaways: Differentiate action log probabilities, not the sample itself.
Estimator correctness and estimator variance are separate issues.

references.title: Spinning Up: Intro to Policy Optimization
references.note: Derive the log-probability gradient and action-independent baseline.

title: Advantages, Baselines, and Variance Reduction
summary: Compare an outcome with an appropriate expectation to reduce noise in policy updates.

sections.title: Relative success is more informative
paragraphs: A reward of ten may be excellent in one state and disappointing in another. A baseline estimates the outcome expected from the current situation, and the advantage measures how much better or worse an action performed. In value notation, \(A^\pi(s,a)=Q^\pi(s,a)-V^\pi(s)\). This does not redefine what the task ultimately rewards. It changes how the policy gradient attributes a sampled outcome relative to the state it began from.

sections.title: Why a state baseline can cancel
paragraphs: For an action-independent \(b(s)\), the expected score-function term \(b(s)\mathbb{E}_a[\nabla\log\pi(a\mid s)]\) is zero under standard regularity assumptions. Subtracting such a baseline therefore need not change the expected policy gradient. It can reduce variance if it predicts returns well. A learned critic estimates \(V(s)\), while Monte Carlo returns or temporal-difference combinations provide targets. Approximate advantage estimators introduce their own bias-variance trade-offs and should not all be described as exactly unbiased.

sections.title: Avoid subtle implementation leaks
paragraphs: Detach advantage values in the actor loss when treating them as fixed weights. Train the critic through its own objective. A baseline that depends on the sampled action can bias a naive estimator, and using a batch mean that includes the same sample requires care. Normalizing advantages changes scale and may affect finite-sample behavior; record the convention. Examine critic error and advantage distributions, especially when rewards are sparse or prompts vary greatly in difficulty.

sections.title: Reading the derivation: what a baseline is allowed to depend on
paragraphs: In Spinning Up's baseline derivation, identify the zero-expectation score-function term. A baseline can depend on the state while remaining independent of the sampled action conditional on that state. This condition explains the unbiasedness argument rather than merely prescribing a subtraction trick.

Suppose an episode receives reward five in a state where typical return is four. Its positive residual is one, smaller than the raw reward but still favorable. If a different state's typical return is eight, the same five is unfavorable. A useful baseline provides this contextual comparison without changing the target expectation.

Check whether baseline fitting leaks the evaluated sample's own action-dependent reward into its estimate. A leave-one-out construction and a mean including that sample have different finite-sample properties. For learned critics, inspect prediction error and stop-gradient handling separately; subtracting an inaccurate baseline may preserve unbiasedness under the assumptions while failing to reduce variance.

exercise.prompt: A state has estimated value 3, and a sampled action has estimated return 5. What advantage is used in the simple difference estimate?
exercise.answer: The advantage is \(5-3=2\), suggesting the sampled action did better than expected from that state. The positive sign raises its probability in an ascent-style policy update, assuming the estimate is treated as fixed.

takeaways: A baseline should match the conditioning of the decision.
Action dependence and gradient flow require explicit care.

title: PPO Ratios, Clipping, and KL Penalties
summary: PPO moderates policy updates using data from a rollout policy, but clipping is not a hard global trust-region guarantee.

sections.title: Compare new and rollout probabilities
paragraphs: Let \(\pi_{\text{old}}\) be the policy that collected the rollout and \(\pi_\theta\) the policy being updated. The ratio \(r=\frac{\pi_\theta(a\mid s)}{\pi_{\text{old}}(a\mid s)}\) indicates how much the probability of a sampled action has changed. PPO's clipped surrogate maximizes the expectation of \(\min\!\left(rA,\operatorname{clip}(r,1-\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon)A\right)\). Old log probabilities and advantages are normally fixed during these updates. The ratio is about data collection, not necessarily about a separate pretrained reference model.

sections.title: Check both advantage signs
paragraphs: For \(A=2\), \(r=1.4\), and \(\varepsilon=0.2\), the unclipped value is 2.8 while the clipped value is 2.4, so the objective uses 2.4. Further increasing that favorable action's ratio receives no extra benefit from this sample's clipped term. For negative advantage, the relevant limiting side reverses. The minimum matters: replacing the objective with a casually clipped gradient does not implement the same function. Multiple minibatch updates reuse the rollout while trying to limit destructive drift.

sections.title: Monitor what clipping cannot promise
paragraphs: Clipping does not enforce that every action probability or the full policy KL remains within a bound. Other samples and shared parameters can move a ratio outside the interval. KL penalties or early stopping may provide additional control, but they are separate choices. In language-model alignment, KL to a fixed reference policy often discourages drift from pretrained behavior; distinguish that reference from the old rollout policy. Log ratio distributions, clip fractions, reward, and KL together instead of trusting one scalar loss.

sections.title: Reading the paper: clipping is sign dependent
paragraphs: In Proximal Policy Optimization Algorithms, read the minimum of the unclipped and clipped objectives literally. The selected branch depends on the advantage sign. The stored rollout policy in the denominator is also distinct from a fixed reference model used for a separate regularization term.

For a positive advantage, increasing an already-too-large ratio stops improving this sample's clipped objective. For a negative advantage, reducing an already-too-small ratio similarly reaches a flat branch. Moves in the harmful direction can remain penalized. This is not equivalent to clamping every probability change in the model.

Plot both branches for one positive and one negative advantage before implementing the loss. Keep the old log probabilities fixed throughout the update window and inspect empirical KL after updates. Shared parameters couple many samples, so clipping a local surrogate does not guarantee that the overall policy remains inside a particular KL radius.

exercise.prompt: With \(A=-2\), \(r=0.5\), and \(\varepsilon=0.2\), what is the clipped surrogate value?
exercise.answer: The two terms are \(-1\) and \(-1.6\), so the minimum is \(-1.6\). This removes the incentive from this term to keep decreasing the probability of the negatively advantaged action beyond the lower clipping boundary.

takeaways: Keep old rollout and fixed reference policies distinct.
Clipping limits an incentive, not every possible policy change.

title: GRPO and RLOO
summary: Group-based reward comparisons can replace a learned value baseline, but the resulting estimators are not identical.

sections.title: Compare several responses to one prompt
paragraphs: Sampling multiple completions for the same prompt provides a local comparison set. In a common GRPO formulation, each response reward is centered by the group's mean and scaled by its standard deviation, producing a group-relative advantage. RLOO uses the mean reward of the other responses as a leave-one-out baseline. Both can avoid training a separate value network, but they differ in normalization, estimator construction, and the policy objective used around that signal.

sections.title: Calculate the relative scores
paragraphs: For rewards \([1,3,5]\), the ordinary group mean is 3, so centered values are \([-2,0,2]\). GRPO-style normalization additionally divides by a declared standard-deviation estimate, usually with numerical stabilization. For the response with reward 1, the RLOO baseline is \(\frac{3+5}{2}=4\), producing advantage \(-3\). For independent completions conditional on the prompt, excluding the current response prevents its reward from entering its own baseline, supporting the standard score-function baseline argument.

sections.title: State the exact variant
paragraphs: GRPO implementations vary in token versus sequence aggregation, clipping, KL terms, length normalization, and reward scaling. RLOO can also be embedded in different optimization pipelines. Report those choices instead of treating the acronym as a complete algorithm. Groups with identical rewards have no within-group ranking signal; near-zero standard deviation needs careful handling. A large group costs generation compute, and relative comparison does not make an unreliable reward correct. Test on a simple reward function before trusting long reasoning rollouts.

sections.title: Reading the papers: compare the actual baseline formulas
paragraphs: Read DeepSeekMath's group-relative advantages beside Back to Basics: Revisiting REINFORCE Style Optimization's leave-one-out construction. Both use multiple responses to a prompt, but group standardization and a baseline formed from the other responses are not the same estimator.

For \(k\) responses, subtracting the others' mean gives \(\frac{k}{k-1}\) times the residual from the full-group mean. At \(k=2\), the first response's advantage is exactly its reward minus the second response's reward. Dividing by the group's estimated standard deviation adds another random, reward-dependent factor and can change optimization weighting.

State independence assumptions, group size, standard-deviation convention, and treatment of equal-reward groups. With independent responses for a fixed prompt, the other responses can provide an action-independent baseline for the selected response. That argument does not automatically establish unbiasedness for every standardized, clipped, token-normalized, or reused-rollout variant carrying the same algorithm name.

exercise.prompt: For rewards \([0,0,1,1]\), what is the RLOO advantage of a response receiving 1?
exercise.answer: The other rewards average \(\frac{0+0+1}{3}=\frac{1}{3}\), so the advantage is \(\frac{2}{3}\). This differs from subtracting the full-group mean, which would give \(\frac{1}{2}\), and from standard-deviation normalization.

takeaways: Group centering and leave-one-out baselines are different.
Record reward normalization and token aggregation explicitly.

title: Direct Preference Optimization
summary: DPO adjusts relative response likelihoods from preference pairs while using a reference policy to anchor the comparison.

sections.title: Start with a preferred pair
paragraphs: For prompt \(x\), let \(y_w\) be a preferred response and \(y_l\) a rejected response. DPO trains a policy directly from such pairs without requiring a separately trained reward model in its standard workflow. The reference policy supplies a baseline likelihood for each response. The learning signal concerns how the new policy changes the preferred-versus-rejected odds relative to that reference, rather than merely maximizing the preferred response's probability in isolation.

sections.title: Read the loss term by term
paragraphs: A standard loss is \(-\log\sigma\!\left(\beta\left[\left(\log\pi_\theta(y_w\mid x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_w\mid x)\right)-\left(\log\pi_\theta(y_l\mid x)-\log\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}(y_l\mid x)\right)\right]\right)\). Sequence log probabilities usually sum token log probabilities with appropriate masks. The reference is fixed, while the policy is optimized. If policy and reference initially agree, the bracket is zero and the loss is \(\log 2\). Raising the preferred response's relative log probability lowers the loss, as does lowering the rejected response's relative log probability.

sections.title: Respect the data and derivation
paragraphs: Preference labels may reflect presentation style, incomplete judgments, or conflicts between annotators. DPO does not turn them into objective truth. The usual method is offline on a preference dataset; generating new pairs during training changes the collection protocol. \(\beta\) controls the reference-relative formulation and should be interpreted within that objective, not as an interchangeable generic learning rate. Audit length effects, masking, and reference consistency. Evaluate generated responses independently because improved pairwise training loss does not guarantee improvement on unseen prompts.

sections.title: Reading the paper: the reference ratio changes the comparison
paragraphs: In Direct Preference Optimization, trace the reparameterization from a reward to a policy-to-reference log ratio. The final pairwise objective compares how much the policy changes the preferred response relative to how much it changes the rejected response. Raw policy likelihoods alone do not express that comparison.

Suppose both responses become twice as likely relative to the reference. Their log-ratio difference remains unchanged, so this preference pair provides no distinction between those equal multiplicative shifts. If only the preferred response gains that factor, the margin increases by \(\beta\log 2\).

Compute sequence log probabilities using consistent prompt masks, termination handling, and tokenizer conventions. The theoretical formulation uses sequence probabilities; replacing sums with length-normalized means changes the objective. DPO avoids explicit reward-model fitting in its standard offline training form, but its result still depends on preference quality, reference coverage, and the distribution represented by the dataset.

exercise.prompt: At initialization \(\pi_\theta=\pi_{\mathrm{ref}}\) for both responses. What is the predicted preference sigmoid argument and loss?
exercise.answer: The argument is zero because both reference-relative log ratios vanish. The sigmoid is 0.5 and the negative log loss is \(\log 2\), approximately 0.693 with natural logarithms.

takeaways: DPO learns reference-relative preference odds.
Offline preference fitting still requires independent generation evaluation.

title: RLHF and RL with Verifiable Rewards
summary: The source and reliability of the reward determine what policy optimization can actually encourage.

sections.title: Two ways to obtain feedback
paragraphs: RLHF commonly uses human judgments, often distilled into a learned reward or preference model, to guide a policy. RL with verifiable rewards uses a procedure that can check some outcome, such as unit tests, exact arithmetic answers, or a constrained game objective. These describe reward sources rather than one mandatory optimizer. Both may use similar policy-gradient machinery, and a system can combine human and automatically checked feedback.

sections.title: Examine what the verifier proves
paragraphs: A code solution that passes five tests has satisfied those tests, not every possible specification. An exact final-answer checker verifies the final value under its parsing rules, not necessarily the reasoning path. Verifiers can be deterministic yet incomplete, vulnerable to formatting exploits, or misaligned with user intent. Human judgments can evaluate nuance that is difficult to automate, but may be noisy, inconsistent, or sensitive to style. The correct comparison depends on the task's measurable properties.

sections.title: Separate training reward from evaluation
paragraphs: Create held-out prompts and, where possible, independent tests or judgments. Inspect high-reward failures and compare them with ordinary outputs. Report reward definitions, parser rules, test coverage, and how invalid responses are handled. A rising training reward can reflect better task performance, better exploitation of a shortcut, or both. Do not label a method reasoning-capable solely because it maximizes a narrow verifier. Document which aspects of correctness remain outside the reward and evaluate those aspects separately.

sections.title: Reading the papers: verification defines the reward's scope
paragraphs: Compare the preference-based reward model in InstructGPT with the rule-based accuracy and format rewards described in DeepSeek-R1. The reward source and policy optimizer are separate design choices. A deterministic scoring function can be convenient without covering every aspect of the intended task.

Consider a programming solution that passes a small set of visible tests but fails an unseen edge case. The reward correctly reports success on those tests; interpreting it as universal program correctness would be the mistake. Similarly, matching a final mathematical answer need not validate every intermediate claim.

Inspect the verifier's accepted formats, tolerances, hidden tests, and failure handling. Evaluate with independent checks where possible, and distinguish accuracy reward from formatting reward when analyzing gains. Verifiability describes an available check under explicit assumptions; it does not eliminate dataset ambiguity, incomplete coverage, or the possibility that optimization exploits weaknesses in the check.

exercise.prompt: A policy learns to print a hidden test result string without solving the requested problem. Is a deterministic checker sufficient protection?
exercise.answer: No. Determinism only makes the check repeatable. If the check rewards the string rather than the intended behavior, optimization can exploit that mismatch. The verifier and independent evaluation need to test the actual task.

takeaways: Reward source and optimization algorithm are separate axes.
Verification coverage limits the claim of correctness.

title: Sampling Temperature, Entropy, and Exploration
summary: Broader sampling can reveal useful alternatives, but randomness alone does not guarantee productive exploration.

sections.title: Explore the policy's alternatives
paragraphs: A policy must sometimes sample choices whose value is uncertain to discover better behavior. In a language model, temperature changes the distribution from which tokens are drawn. For positive \(T\), \(p_T(a)\) is proportional to \(\exp(z_a/T)\). Higher temperature generally spreads probability more broadly, while lower temperature concentrates it. Entropy \(H(\pi)=-\sum_a\pi(a)\log\pi(a)\) measures uncertainty in a distribution; it is a property of the probabilities, not a direct measure of task competence.

sections.title: Connect sampling to the estimator
paragraphs: With probabilities \([0.9,0.1]\), the rarer action is seldom observed but may lead to a higher reward. More exploration can reveal that possibility. However, top-k or top-p truncation may remove actions from support, preventing their discovery entirely. If rollouts use a modified sampling distribution, policy-gradient log probabilities and correction terms must match the intended estimator. Computing log probabilities under an unmodified distribution while sampling under another can silently change the training objective.

sections.title: Balance diversity and useful feedback
paragraphs: High-temperature samples may become invalid and receive identical low rewards, producing little informative ranking. An entropy bonus encourages distributional spread during optimization, whereas sampling temperature modifies collection or generation; these are different interventions. Track invalid rates, reward variance, duplicate responses, and task success alongside entropy. Exploration budgets also include the number of prompts and completions. Evaluate at a fixed decoding protocol so an apparent training gain is not merely a change in inference-time sampling or number of attempts.

sections.title: Reading the sources: sampling and regularization change different objects
paragraphs: Use the entropy definition in Deep Learning and the policy-gradient formulation in Spinning Up to distinguish a distribution's uncertainty from a training bonus. Sampling temperature transforms the behavior distribution, while an entropy regularizer contributes an additional term to the optimized objective.

Suppose logits define probabilities \([0.9,0.1]\), but collection uses a different temperature. Recording the original probabilities as though they generated the actions gives incorrect behavior log probabilities for importance ratios. Top-k truncation creates an additional issue: excluded actions have zero behavior probability, so support can disappear.

Log the exact sampling transformation used for rollout collection, including renormalization and truncation. Evaluate diversity and task reward together because random variation is not automatically useful exploration. If an entropy bonus is used, specify its coefficient and whether it is computed over the full or truncated distribution; those choices can optimize different policies.

exercise.prompt: A top-k sampler excludes an action with high true reward. Can temperature alone rediscover it while the action remains excluded?
exercise.answer: No. An action with zero sampling support cannot be drawn, regardless of temperature applied within the retained set. Exploration requires changing the support or using another collection mechanism.

takeaways: Match log probabilities to the sampling mechanism.
Diversity is useful only when it exposes informative alternatives.

title: Reward Hacking and Distribution Shift
summary: Optimization can exploit weaknesses in a reward proxy as the policy moves beyond the data that shaped it.

sections.title: A proxy becomes a target
paragraphs: A reward is usually an operational measurement of a broader goal. If a writing reward correlates with answer length, a policy may become verbose without becoming more helpful. This is reward hacking: behavior improves the measured signal while missing the intended objective. It need not involve deliberate intent by the model. Repeated optimization naturally searches for actions that score well, including regions where the reward model is poorly supported.

sections.title: Follow the shifting data
paragraphs: A reward model may be trained on ordinary assistant responses, then evaluate increasingly unusual policy-generated outputs. The resulting input distribution differs from its training distribution. An initially harmless correlation can become a shortcut under optimization. For example, a model that predicts correctness partly from confident language may assign high scores to confident false statements after the policy learns that pattern. More reward optimization can therefore reduce genuine quality even while the reported reward rises.

sections.title: Build independent diagnostics
paragraphs: Keep evaluation labels or tests independent of the optimized reward when possible. Examine the highest-scoring outputs, stratify by length and format, and create adversarial cases that isolate suspected shortcuts. Monitor reward and task success on the same held-out trajectories. Updating the reward model with new examples may help, but also changes the training system and should be documented. Constraints and reference regularization can limit drift, yet they do not prove that the reward captures the goal. Treat a widening reward-quality gap as a measurement problem requiring investigation.

sections.title: Reading the paper: stronger optimization can expose the proxy
paragraphs: In Scaling Laws for Reward Model Overoptimization, inspect proxy reward and the separate evaluation reward as optimization strength changes. The paper's experimental gold reward is itself a stronger learned model, not direct access to perfect human judgment. That distinction limits what the plotted separation proves.

Imagine a reward model that associates unusually long answers with quality. Policy optimization can increase length beyond the range represented in its training data, raising the proxy while making answers repetitive. This is both an exploit of a learned correlation and a shift in the model's input distribution.

Test the hypothesized shortcut directly: compare length-matched answers, blinded judgments, and independently specified task checks. Preserve reward and quality curves separately instead of stopping analysis at the training objective. Regularization or early stopping may limit exploitation, but neither repairs an incomplete definition of success or guarantees reliability under a new distribution.

exercise.prompt: Training reward increases while independent human preference falls. What should you conclude first?
exercise.answer: The reward is no longer a reliable proxy on the current policy distribution, or the evaluation protocols differ in a consequential way. Inspect both measurement processes and concrete outputs before claiming the policy improved.

takeaways: Optimization exposes weaknesses in imperfect proxies.
Evaluate the policy with evidence beyond its training reward.

title: On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning
summary: The relationship between the data-generating policy and the optimized policy determines what corrections or assumptions are needed.

sections.title: Identify behavior and target policies
paragraphs: The behavior policy generates the data. The target policy is the policy whose performance or gradient is being estimated. On-policy methods primarily use trajectories from the current target policy or a closely controlled recent version. Off-policy methods learn from data generated by another policy, including older policies or demonstrations. These categories concern distributions, not whether data came from the internet, a simulator, or a live robot.

sections.title: See why naive reuse changes an expectation
paragraphs: For a single action at a fixed state, an expectation under \(\pi\) can sometimes be estimated from actions sampled under \(\mu\) using importance weight \(\frac{\pi(a\mid s)}{\mu(a\mid s)}\), provided \(\mu\) covers \(\pi\)'s support. A full-trajectory likelihood ratio is the product of per-step action ratios when the initial-state and environment dynamics are shared; it already accounts for the induced state-distribution change, but its variance can be severe. Methods that avoid that product need their own corrections or assumptions. A one-step ratio does not turn every stale trajectory into an unbiased estimate of every desired quantity.

sections.title: Place common training loops carefully
paragraphs: PPO collects rollouts with an old policy and performs limited updates using probability ratios; it is commonly grouped with on-policy methods despite this controlled reuse. A large replay buffer mixes older behavior distributions and is characteristic of many off-policy methods. Offline RL uses a fixed dataset and faces support limitations; ordinary SFT on demonstrations is supervised imitation, not automatically an off-policy RL algorithm. Record behavior-policy versions, sampling settings, reuse counts, and support restrictions to make these distinctions concrete.

sections.title: Reading the sources: a trajectory ratio already includes its states
paragraphs: Read Spinning Up's algorithm taxonomy alongside the trajectory factorization in its policy-gradient derivation. With shared initial-state distribution and environment transitions, dividing target and behavior trajectory probabilities cancels those common factors. The remaining product of action ratios already accounts for which states are visited.

For two steps with ratios two and three, the trajectory weight is six, not an average of 2.5. Extending such products over long horizons can produce extreme weights and high variance. A one-step ratio is cheaper but does not generally replace the full correction for an arbitrary trajectory-level expectation.

Check support before arithmetic: an action impossible under the behavior policy cannot be recovered by ordinary importance weighting. State whether a method uses full products, value-learning assumptions, or controlled recent-policy reuse such as PPO. The phrase off-policy describes a distributional relationship, not a guarantee that any stored interaction can be reused without qualification.

exercise.prompt: The target policy assigns positive probability to an action to which the behavior policy assigns probability zero. Can ordinary importance weighting recover that action's contribution from behavior-policy data?
exercise.answer: No. The ratio is undefined on missing support, and the data contain no observations of that action. Additional exploration, modeling assumptions, or a constrained target policy is needed.

takeaways: Name the behavior and target distributions.
Support mismatch cannot be fixed by a ratio alone.

title: Credit Assignment Across a Trajectory
summary: A final outcome must be connected to the earlier decisions that helped or harmed it.

sections.title: Delayed feedback hides causality
paragraphs: A robot may fail only after a long sequence of movements, or a generated answer may be marked wrong after hundreds of tokens. The final reward does not directly identify the decisive earlier choice. Credit assignment asks which actions should change and by how much. Assigning the same terminal return to every action is a valid starting estimator in suitable episodic settings, but its variance and interpretability can be poor.

sections.title: Use temporal structure
paragraphs: Reward-to-go excludes rewards that occurred before an action because that action cannot affect the past. A value baseline removes predictable state-level outcomes. Temporal-difference methods compare an observed reward plus estimated next value with the current value estimate. These tools exploit structure to improve learning signals, but estimated values introduce approximation and sometimes bias. In language generation, a local token may matter through later consequences, so token-level correctness labels and sequence-level reward are not interchangeable.

sections.title: Avoid causal stories from one success
paragraphs: A successful trajectory contains useful decisions, irrelevant details, and sometimes recoverable mistakes. Reinforcing every visible pattern can reward accidental correlations. Compare alternative actions or carefully designed ablations where possible, and inspect failure timing. Dense intermediate rewards can help learning but may redirect behavior if they are poorly aligned with the final goal. Document shaping rules and evaluate the unshaped task objective. For long-horizon problems, better state representations and memory may be as important as changing the gradient estimator.

sections.title: Reading the derivation: remove rewards that the action cannot cause
paragraphs: In Spinning Up's reward-to-go derivation, inspect why past rewards multiply a score-function term with zero expectation. Removing those terms can reduce variance while preserving the expected policy gradient under the stated assumptions. This is a causal and probabilistic argument, not a claim that every token has a known individual contribution.

Consider a three-action episode with rewards \([2,0,5]\) after the respective actions and no discounting. Full-episode return is seven for every action, while reward-to-go values are seven, five, and five. The last action should not receive extra sampling noise from a reward already realized before it was chosen.

For a terminal-only response reward, all earlier actions can still receive that outcome through a valid trajectory estimator. The difficulty is variance and attribution, not the absence of a gradient formula. Additional process rewards or shaping terms require validation because changing the reward can change which behavior is optimal.

exercise.prompt: An action at time 5 receives a gradient weight containing a reward from time 2. Why can that term be removed in the usual policy-gradient derivation?
exercise.answer: The later action cannot cause the earlier reward. Under the standard conditional expectation argument, its score-function contribution for past rewards has zero expectation, so removing it can reduce unnecessary variance.

takeaways: Terminal success does not identify each action's contribution.
Temporal structure can reduce noise without changing the intended goal.
